method.quote: 'Magnetic beneficiation should extract most of the free ferromagnetic metal grains (iron, nickel, and cobalt) from the silicate and carbonaceous grains.'
method.note: Kargel 1994 likewise proposes that pulverised LL-chondrite regolith be 'electromagnetically raked' to separate metal grains (search excerpt). NASA SP-509 vol.3 notes metal is the 'magnetically separable (metallic) component' (https://nss.org/settlement/nasa/spaceresvol3/asterres1c.htm).

recovery_fraction.note: No asteroid-mining study with a stated numeric magnetic recovery fraction was found; sources say only 'most'. Elvis 2014: 'Resource extraction efficiency ... is unlikely to be 100%, especially at first'.

lab_example_H5_magnetic_fraction.unit: wt% of bulk recovered as clean metal
lab_example_H5_magnetic_fraction.quote: 'We crushed the sample in an agate mortar and separated the magnetic (metal) from the non-magnetic (stone) fraction ... we obtained 33 mg of relatively clean metal, corresponding to 13.9 wt% bulk metal.'
lab_example_H5_magnetic_fraction.note: Hand magnet lab prep on an H5 chondrite (Arpu Kuilpu); vs ~18.5 wt% average H metal this is roughly 75% recovered, but that ratio is DERIVED across different samples, not a stated recovery.

areal_mass_direct_figure.note: No fetched source states a typical kg/m2 for airliner fuselage shells. A search summary attributed '5.0 lb/sq ft' (24.4 kg/m2 of wetted area, transport fuselage) to Raymer but the page was not verified.

areal_mass_formula_AA241.unit: lb, with S_fuse in ft2 (so the bracket is lb/ft2 of wetted area)
areal_mass_formula_AA241.quote: Stanford AA241 (Kroo): 'Fuselage weight is based on gross fuselage wetted area ... and upon a pressure-bending load parameter. The pressure index is: Ip = 1.5E-3 * P * B ... W fuse = (1.051 + .102 * I fuse) * S fuse. Subtract 8.5% for all-cargo aircraft.'
areal_mass_formula_AA241.note: Floor of 1.051 lb/ft2 = 5.1 kg/m2; P in lb/ft2, B width in ft. For P = 8.6 psi and B = 20 ft, Ip = 37 giving ~4.8 lb/ft2 = 24 kg/m2 (DERIVED example).

factor_of_safety_limit_to_ultimate.quote: 14 CFR 25.303: 'Unless otherwise specified, a factor of safety of 1.5 must be applied to the prescribed limit load which are considered external loads on the structure.'

pressure_cabin_factor.quote: 14 CFR 25.365(d): 'withstand the pressure differential loads corresponding to the maximum relief valve setting multiplied by a factor of 1.33 for airplanes to be approved for operation to 45,000 feet or by a factor of 1.67 for airplanes to be approved for operation above 45,000 feet, omitting other loads.'
pressure_cabin_factor.note: These are limit-load factors; 25.303's 1.5 applies on top (1.33 x 1.5 = 2.0 ultimate), matching Wikipedia Factor_of_safety: 'for pressurized fuselage it is 2.0, and for main landing gear structures it is often 1.25'.

cabin_pressure_differential.quote: 'typical values are between 540 hPa (7.8 psi) and 650 hPa (9.4 psi)'
